analysis.one_liner: Phases out 'forever chemicals' from manufacturing, consumer products, and federal purchasing over ten years.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with 7 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to five House committees and has seen no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: PFAS chemicals, called 'forever chemicals' because they never break down, are found in the blood of nearly all Americans and contaminate drinking water across the country. This bill would require manufacturers to report every use of PFAS, ban nonessential uses within ten years, take specific products like carpets, cosmetics, and food packaging off store shelves on faster timelines, stop the government from buying PFAS-containing products, and give the EPA new enforcement powers including citizen lawsuits. It has been referred to five House committees and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to PFAS through drinking water, food packaging, clothing, and household products; communities near PFAS manufacturing and release sites; and people whose exposure-related lawsuits are currently cut short by corporate bankruptcy filings.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every manufacturer and user of PFAS to file annual public reports on volumes, releases, health effects, and exposed workers, and bans all nonessential uses within 10 years of enactment [S2] [S3].

Bans specific consumer products containing PFAS on staggered timelines — carpets, food packaging, and juvenile products within 1 year; cosmetics and indoor furniture within 2 years; outdoor apparel for severe wet conditions within 5 years [S2] [S3].

Imposes a 10-year phaseout of any release of PFAS above detection levels, backed by civil penalties, criminal penalties of up to 5 years' imprisonment, inspections, and citizen suits against manufacturers, users, and the EPA itself [S2] [S3].

Requires federal agencies to stop procuring PFAS-containing products where practicable, waives federal immunity so agencies are subject to the same PFAS laws as private parties (with a narrow national-security exemption the President must report to Congress), and exempts PFAS liability claims from bankruptcy stays so victims can still pursue non-debtor companies [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: PFAS manufacturers and the many product industries that use the chemicals — textiles, cosmetics, food packaging, carpets, and oil and gas — face mandatory reformulation, reporting fees, and liability; some costs would likely pass through to consumers as higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Chemical makers and consumer product companies

drawbacks.text: Compliance and reformulation costs for manufacturers of carpets, clothing, cosmetics, and packaged food would likely be passed partly to consumers through higher prices, and some products may be pulled from the market before adequate substitutes exist [S3].

Some PFAS uses have no proven safer alternatives — the bill handles this through a National Academies-reviewed 'essential use' designation process, but that review can take up to 3 years, leaving regulated industries and their workers in a long period of uncertainty [S2] [S3].

The eventual ban on any release of PFAS 'above the threshold of detection' is a near-zero-emissions standard that may be technically difficult or impossible for some facilities to meet, raising the risk of chronic violation and enforcement disputes [S3].

The bankruptcy provision lets claimants pursue non-debtor parent companies and affiliates after a PFAS defendant files for bankruptcy, which manufacturers argue could disrupt orderly bankruptcy resolutions and impose open-ended liability on corporate families [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health stakes are large and real: PFAS do not break down, accumulate in the body, and are linked to serious health harms, so phasing out nonessential uses addresses a problem that gets worse every year it is left alone. The main honest costs are transition disruption for industries with no ready substitutes, possible consumer price increases, and a deliberately strict enforcement regime. The bill's design mitigates the first concern through an essential-use exemption process, so on balance the benefits plausibly outweigh the costs — but none of that matters while the bill sits without action.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2026 and referred to five House committees, with one subcommittee referral the next day; no hearing, markup, or vote has taken place since [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Betty McCollum (D-MN), joined by Rep. Morrison, introduced the Forever Chemical Regulation and Accountability Act of 2026 on March 19, 2026 [S1] [S3].

The bill was referred to five committees — Energy and Commerce, Oversight and Government Reform, Science, Space, and Technology, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Armed Services — and then to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee on March 20, 2026 [S1] [S5].
The bill has 7 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no recorded committee action, floor debate, or vote [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, PFAS manufacturers and PFAS-using product industries, which continue business as usual with no new restrictions or liability while the bill sits in committee.

for.name: Betty McCollum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and secured 7 Democratic cosponsors

for.name: Kelly Morrison
for.role: U.S. Representative, MN; original cosponsor who joined in introducing the bill
for.what_they_did: Joined McCollum in introducing the bill on the floor

for.name: 7 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction

against.name: House committee chairs (Energy and Commerce, Transportation and Infrastructure, Armed Services, Oversight, Science)
against.role: Chairs of the five committees of referral
against.what_they_did: No committee has scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill since its referral in March 2026; under House rules nothing moves without a committee action or a leadership decision to bring it up

against.name: PFAS manufacturers and PFAS-using industries
against.role: Chemical producers and makers of carpets, textiles, cosmetics, food packaging, and oil and gas products
against.what_they_did: The bill would cost these industries billions in reformulation, reporting fees, and liability; such industries routinely lobby against PFAS restrictions, though no lobbying on this specific bill appears in the record

sides.party_line_note: All 8 supporters (the sponsor and 7 cosponsors) are Democrats; Republicans hold the House majority and control the committees where the bill sits, and no Republican has signed on.

industries.note: The bill bans nonessential production within 10 years, prohibits nearly all releases, requires costly annual reporting and fees, and allows citizen suits and criminal penalties. Its interest in continuing to sell PFAS runs directly against the public's interest in ending exposure to persistent toxic chemicals.

industries.industry: Consumer product makers (textiles, cosmetics, food packaging, carpets, furniture)
industries.note: Mandatory staggered sales bans would force these companies to reformulate or drop PFAS-treated products within 1 to 5 years. Their interest in using cheap, effective PFAS coatings conflicts with consumers' interest in not absorbing these chemicals through food, clothing, and homes.

PFAS-containing oil and gas products would be banned from sale within 1 year. The industry's interest in continued use runs against public exposure reduction, though the specific effect here is narrower than the sector-wide stakes of other PFAS rules.

Federal agencies must stop procuring PFAS-containing products and become subject to state and federal PFAS law like private parties, ending a major source of exposure near military installations; but the President retains a renewable national-security exemption, and defense suppliers with no substitutes face compliance costs.

industries.industry: Water utilities and waste treatment facilities
industries.note: The bill explicitly excludes public water systems and treatment works from the definition of regulated 'manufacturer' and 'user,' shielding passive receivers of PFAS from liability while requiring polluters to pay.

analysis.trajectory: Bills with no majority-party support and referrals to five committees rarely advance; with roughly nine months left in this Congress, the realistic path is that the bill dies in committee at the end of the session unless it gains bipartisan sponsorship or a vehicle outside the regular committee process.
